analysis.one_liner: Taxes 90% of oil producers' crisis-era windfall profits to fund energy aid for poor households.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: After Iraq's invasion of Kuwait sent oil prices sharply upward in 1990, this bill would have imposed an excise tax equal to 90% of any oil producer's or importer's profits per barrel above what it earned before the crisis. Two-thirds of the revenue would go to the Treasury and one-third to a dedicated trust fund for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance program and home weatherization, with the tax expiring after four to six quarters. The bill was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, but none of them acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households would gain: the trust fund would send money, without further annual appropriations, to the federal grant program that helps poor families pay heating and utility bills (LIHEAP) and to the weatherization program that insulates low-income homes, with a floor of $1.5 billion and $200 million in direct appropriations required before trust fund dollars could flow [S3]. The federal Treasury would also keep the other 67% of the tax revenue [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households facing high energy bills

how_it_helps.text: The bill taxes 90% of the 'windfall profit' on each barrel — the excess of the producer's or importer's gross profit per barrel over its average per-barrel profit during the four months ending July 31, 1990, before the price spike [S3].

It creates a Low Income Energy Support Trust Fund funded by 33% of the windfall tax receipts, with 7/8 of each quarter's allocation going to the LIHEAP grant program for poor households' energy bills and 1/8 to the home weatherization program [S2][S3].

The trust fund money is supplemental to direct appropriations and cannot be spent unless Congress directly appropriates at least $1.5 billion for LIHEAP and $200 million for weatherization, adjusted for inflation after fiscal 1992 [S3].

The tax is explicitly temporary: it ends after four calendar quarters, or six if the President determines a continuing energy price crisis exists, and can be revived for four quarters by a presidential determination [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Domestic crude oil producers and importers would pay the excise tax — 90 cents of every dollar of per-barrel profit above their pre-crisis average. Some portion of the tax could be passed forward to refiners and ultimately to consumers at the pump, and producers would face an added disincentive to expand output during a supply shortage.

drawbacks.text: A windfall profits tax during a supply crisis can discourage additional domestic production: if new output is taxed at 90% of the profit above a baseline, producers have less reason to drill more barrels precisely when supply is scarce — a criticism that helped lead Congress to repeal the earlier windfall profit tax in 1988.

The tax base is built on reported prices, costs, and a fixed baseline period; producers could restructure sales among related parties, and the bill attempts to police this by requiring fair-market pricing in related-party sales, but administration would be complex [S3].
Some of the tax could be shifted to refiners and consumers, partially offsetting the aid the bill provides to households facing higher energy prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a temporary, targeted response to a specific price shock: take the profit surge off the top of oil producers and put a third of it into heating assistance and weatherization for the poor. Its main weaknesses are the classic ones for windfall taxes — the possibility of pass-through to consumers, a chilling effect on new production during a shortage, and administrative complexity. Because it expired after four to six quarters and required substantial direct appropriations before trust-fund money flowed, its fiscal exposure was limited. On balance, the benefits to vulnerable households during a price spike outweighed the risks, though honest supporters would concede the tax might have partially reached consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced and then to two subcommittees, but no committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Silvio Conte introduced the bill on September 27, 1990, about two months after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait sent oil prices sharply upward, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Energy and Commerce committees [S1][S5].
On October 15, 1990, it was referred to the Energy and Power Subcommittee, and on October 26, 1990, to the Human Resources Subcommittee [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, markups, votes, or floor consideration — and the Congress ended on January 3, 1991, killing the bill [S1][S5].
The bill drew only four cosponsors: three House Democrats and one House Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers and importers came out ahead: they kept the full windfall profits from the 1990–91 oil price spike instead of paying 90% of the excess above their pre-crisis baseline. Low-income households did not receive the dedicated trust-fund boost to heating assistance and weatherization the bill would have provided.

for.name: Rep. Silvio O. Conte
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Petroleum Producers Burden Sharing Act on September 27, 1990, following the oil price spike after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.

for.name: 3 of 257 House Democrats and 1 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small bipartisan support.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never acted on it; the tax provisions could not move without this committee's approval.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees (Energy and Power; Human Resources) but held no hearings or markups.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with a mix of Democratic and Republican cosponsors, and it never reached a vote, so no party split on its merits appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have taken 90% of every dollar of per-barrel profit above their pre-crisis baseline for up to six quarters [S3]. Their interest in blocking it ran against the low-income households the revenue would have supported, since the tax's whole purpose was to recapture producer windfalls during the price spike and redirect part of them to energy assistance [S2][S3].
Refiners and consumers could face higher crude costs if producers passed part of the tax forward, though the bill also targeted price spikes that raise everyone's energy bills.
